items.en: One self-hosted home for your focus, habits, goals, money and projects — with an MCP server so your AI assistant can work alongside you.
Quick start · Tour · AI / MCP · Deploy · API

Most of us run our lives across a to-do app, a habit tracker, a budgeting spreadsheet, a Pomodoro timer and a notes app — and none of them know about each other. Edi Life OS puts all of it in one calm, private dashboard and connects the small things you do today to the direction you want your life to take.
- Everything in one place. Ten workspaces share one design, one sign-in and one database.
- Connected, not just collected. Habits drive goal progress, Kanban cards show up in the calendar, and the Overview turns it all into one daily score.
- Yours. Runs on any PHP + MySQL host, even cheap shared hosting. No subscription, no tracking, no vendor lock-in.
- AI-ready. A built-in MCP server lets Claude and other assistants read your dashboard, plan goals, log habits and track expenses for you.
Dates follow Asia/Tehran. The weather card shows Qeshm Island via Open-Meteo; its tide figure is a modeled estimate, not for navigation.

Edi Life OS ships with an optional MCP server that exposes 26 tools across your dashboard, goals, tasks, habits, finances and notes. Connect it to Claude Desktop, Claude Code or any MCP client and ask in plain language:
"Create a SMART goal called Build a home studio, due in three months, and add Buy acoustic panels as a task."
"Log a 450,000 Toman food expense and show my balance."
The MCP server talks to your app only through its token-protected HTTP API. It never touches your database or credentials. Setup takes a minute — see MCP server below.
git clone https://github.com/edrisranjbar/lifeos.git && cd lifeos
cp .env.example .env # set your sign-in and passwords
Open localhost:8080 and sign in. MySQL, the app and your attachments each live in their own volume, so docker compose up -d --build after a git pull upgrades without losing data.

Download lifeos-<version>.zip from the latest release and extract it into your hosting home directory, so public_html/ becomes your web root and the backend sits safely above it. Copy config.example.php to config.php, fill in your MySQL details, and open your site. See the deployment guide for details.
You need PHP 8.1+ (with pdo_mysql and mbstring) and MySQL 8+ (or MariaDB 10.4+).
git clone https://github.com/edrisranjbar/lifeos.git
cp config.example.php config.php # PowerShell: Copy-Item config.example.php config.php
Edit config.php with your database connection and the username and password you want to sign in with, then start the server:
php -S localhost:8000 -t public_html server.php
Open localhost:8000 and sign in. The database and tables are created on first use. You can change your sign-in later in Settings.
config.php and .env hold real credentials and are gitignored. Never commit them.
A private /api/v1 API covers the dashboard, goals, tasks, habits, finances and sticky notes. It uses its own bearer token, separate from your browser sign-in.
php -r "echo bin2hex(random_bytes(32));"
Set the result as api_token in config.php (or the LIFEOS_API_TOKEN environment variable), then:
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $LIFEOS_API_TOKEN" https://your-host/api/v1/dashboard
See the API reference for endpoints, payloads and errors.
cp .env.example .env # set LIFEOS_BASE_URL and LIFEOS_API_TOKEN
The server runs over stdio; there is no hosted MCP endpoint. The MCP guide lists every tool and shows client configuration for Claude and Codex.
- Everything lives in your MySQL database. Habits use dedicated tables; other workspaces store JSON documents in app_state .
- Saves use revision checks, so a stale tab can't silently overwrite newer changes. API writes use transactions and row locks.
- Data from older browser-only versions is imported once; conflicting copies are archived as legacy_backup_* records.
- Back up the database, attachment files and your configuration together.
Moving from the old Habittify SQLite database? See migrating Habittify.
Edi Life OS is built for a single owner.
- The API token grants read and write access to every supported domain. Token scopes and app-level rate limiting are not implemented, so set request limits at the hosting layer.
- Use HTTPS anywhere other than localhost, and keep tokens out of URLs, frontend code, screenshots and logs.
- Secret notes are hidden from API reads by default. The secret flag controls visibility; it is not separate encryption.
public_html/ Browser workspaces, shared assets and Apache entry points
lib/ API domains, response helpers and state transactions
tests/ Timer, API, MySQL and integration checks
docs/ Guides, plus README screenshots in docs/media
config.example.php Configuration template (no real credentials)
server.php Development router and application routing
Built with PHP, MySQL and vanilla JavaScript — no frontend build step, no framework.
Dockerfile, docker-compose.yml and docker/config.php run the app with configuration from environment variables.
- API reference — authentication, routes, data formats and concurrency
- MCP guide — tools, environment settings and client setup
- Deployment guide — Apache, shared hosting, backups and migration
- Development guide — local checks and disposable integration fixtures
Ideas, bug reports and pull requests are welcome. Open an issue to start a conversation, and see the development guide to run the checks locally.
If Edi Life OS helps you run your days, consider giving it a ⭐ — it helps others find it.

On Thursday, at the Golden Age of American Innovation Summit, President Trump awarded Elon Musk, Jensen Huang, Sergey Brin, and AMD’s Lisa Su the National Medal of Science, the nation’s top science prize. Dell Technologies’ Michael Dell and Microsoft’s Satya Nadella also received the National Medal of Technology and Innovation.

Together, the awardees have donated nearly $6 billion to efforts tied to Trump and his administration, according to The New Republic. Alphabet and Microsoft, for example, donated to the president’s inauguration fund and White House ballroom. AMD gave to a pro-Trump Super PAC, and Michael and Susan Dell pledged $6.25 billion to help fund the Trump Accounts, the administration’s savings program for children.
Trump said the honorees had helped “pioneer an incredible future for America,” and that because of them, “we will always be on top. No one else can compete with us.”
Nadella received his medal right after the administration indefinitely suspended Microsoft from the H-1B program, which lets U.S. companies hire skilled foreign workers.

Can AI design new life forms? In 2025, Stanford University PhD student Samuel King came up with a preliminary answer when he used a generative AI model to propose genetic blueprints for microscopic viruses. It isn’t yet an example of AI-generated life, but that could be next. Join senior AI reporter James O'Donnell as he interviews King about his work, being named one of MIT Technology Review's Innovators Under 35 and new ways of seeing biology.
Going live on October 16th at 18:30 BST / 1:30pm EDT / 10:30am PDT
Speakers: James O'Donnell, AI Reporter, and Samuel King, Bioengineering PhD Candidate, Stanford University/Arc Institute
Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.
AI’s recursive self-improvement might not come so quickly after all
AI agents are not yet creative enough to carry out genuinely innovative open-ended AI research, it seems.

It’s a rough time to be in the nonprofit sector. For decades, Americans have relied on nonprofits to provide essential services such as food pantries, education, health care, and housing programs, which were often bolstered by government grants and contracts. But much of that money has dried up over the past two years. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act slashed federal spending on health care and food assistance; the Trump administration has also called for contract reviews and spending freezes for nonprofits across the board. “Almost everyone in the industry has seen layoffs,” one housing nonprofit employee told me. “I got a salary reduction, and I don’t know if or when I’ll ever make what I used to — which still wasn’t very much.”

These budget shortfalls put a new level of pressure on nonprofit fundraisers tasked with keeping the lights on. Fundraising, often delicately referred to as “advancement” or “development” in nonprofit parlance, might seem like a cushy job: You get to schmooze with wealthy donors and persuade them to contribute to your cause. But employees hopping between disparate worlds — from incredible need to incredible excess — can find the work head-spinning at best and infuriating at worst. Here, four fundraisers share their stories of code-switching on the job, driven by the egos they have to manage and the desperation they feel to secure major gifts for their organizations.
“Some of our major funders would show up to a food pantry in Prada boots.” — a California-based fundraiser who has worked at nonprofits for more than 15 years

When I graduated from college, I didn’t know what to do with my life. I wound up getting an internship at the private high school I went to in the alumni and development office, which led to an entry-level position on their fundraising team. That’s how I became a frontline fundraiser, as we call ourselves. But it was a rude awakening when I went to my first alumni events. My boss would stand next to me, greeting people at the door, and say to me, “Oh, we need to follow that person because she’s wearing those shoes or that bag.” She was sizing up people so hard. And I was like, Wow, I hate this. It seemed like such a harsh and fast way to decide if that’s a person worth talking to.

As I’ve become more senior in this field, I don’t run my fundraising that way. I make sure we talk to everybody in the room. Wealth indicators are way more advanced than what kind of shoes someone wears. Sometimes the least obvious person in the room is a billionaire. But also, we now have much more advanced tools to identify potential donors. I work for a university now, and we have a whole research team. We use a software called Windfall that essentially functions as a screening engine for people’s money. Using publicly available information — like if someone buys a new home — it tracks our alumni and will rate them based on their profession, where they live, the cost of their house. At one place I worked, we wouldn’t consider someone a major gift prospect if their house was worth less than $4 million. It sounds sneaky, but it’s standard practice across nonprofit development teams. It will even alert you if someone in the database sells a big chunk of stocks because that demonstrates they’re liquid and moving money. The thinking is If money’s going someplace, it might as well come to us.
Of course, these tools are flawed, and they make mistakes. You have to be careful about how you bring up information you have on people because it might be wrong — or it might creep them out.

I do remember the first major gift I secured. I’d been working at a university for three months, and we were doing a campaign where major gifts would be matched. One guy called me and was like, “I’m in for $125,000.” And I remember sitting at my desk like, Holy shit, I did it. That’s a $250,000 gift with the match. I will never forget the feeling of closing that gift, which went to a wonderful scholarship recipient. The whole point of what I was trying to do was create access to this university for people who wouldn’t be able to afford it otherwise.

The relationship between the scholarship recipients and donors can be tricky. Sometimes it’s really beautiful — the donor gets to see them graduate, and they have this gratifying connection. But in other cases, it can be awkward. There was one time when a donor, who was an older white man, got assigned to a young Black woman as the scholarship recipient, and we arranged for them to have coffee. And it was immediately clear he had this white-savior complex. The questions he was asking her and the things he was saying … I was like, “Time to wrap this up!” I shared what happened with our team, and they reassigned the student to a different donor and paired the donor with a different scholarship recipient. But these things are sensitive.

I’ve also worked for a nonprofit that helped people with food insecurity, and some of our major funders would show up to a food pantry in Prada boots. There was a weird lack of touch with reality. I’d go from a golf outing or a huge gala to a mobile pantry with a long line of people who don’t have enough food. The whiplash is real.

“It’s nerve-racking to meet with very wealthy donors.” — Ellen Simmons, the chief advancement officer at Ronald McDonald House of New England, a Boston-based nonprofit providing accommodations to families with children receiving medical treatment far from home

I started out in operations at Ronald McDonald House, working with families directly. I met people whose lives were falling apart because they had a sick child. I remember one mother who flew in from Puerto Rico and didn’t have a place to stay. She sat in my office nursing her baby, begging me for a room, and I didn’t have one available. I don’t know what happened to that mom, and ten years later, it still haunts me. Every night, I know there are families sleeping in their cars, sleeping on floors, or forgoing treatment for their kids because they don’t have accommodations.

Now, as a fundraiser, I deal with the other side of the table — these wealthy individuals who have the ability to help. But it’s a balancing act. I’m not simply telling stories about needy families in a way that makes a donor feel emotional. They’re not just checkbooks, and they’ll smell it a mile away if they’re treated that way. These relationships take time to build. The challenge is these are not my social groups. I did not grow up around these people. So how do we get in the door? How do we become relevant to the people who can afford to give this amount of money?
It does get frustrating sometimes. Like, we need $60 million for our new capital campaign. That’s a ton of money to me, but for some people, it’s a drop in the bucket.

It’s nerve-racking to meet with very wealthy donors. I get nervous every single time I have breakfast with people at The ’Quin House, a private social club in Boston and they’re talking about their kid’s elite soccer team flying to Scotland or taking their private planes to Martha’s Vineyard. I focus on finding commonalities between us, like maybe we both have dogs, we’re both moms. I try not to get hung up on whether I need a new outfit for a big meeting. But it’s not easy. I feel embarrassed sometimes, like Are they going to judge what I’m wearing? Maybe they will. But caring about children and families, that transcends wealth. Everybody knows somebody who has been touched by illness. If I can find that connection, then we’re good.

Nowadays, we can use AI to predict how much a donor might be able to give. We can look up details about donors who give to pediatric causes in the city of Boston. A year ago, I would have felt ethically divided on that. But I come back to the families we serve. I am leaving money on the table if I’m not using every tool out there. But there’s a lot of discretion involved. You can’t just say, “Oh, I saw you went to this university and you have three kids and you just bought a boat.” If you slip up and say something like that, you can kiss that relationship good-bye. But if you ask questions the right way, that information comes out organically and you’re more prepared to run with it when it does.
“Things get messy all the time because you’re dealing with money and power.”— a fundraising consultant who has worked at nonprofits in the tristate area for 20 years

My first internship in the fundraising space, which turned into my first job, was in New York City. And I remember going out to meet with donors on Shelter Island in the Hamptons and it was very intimidating. I learned pretty quickly that fundraising is a lot like sales. I get to sell the best product because I really believe in the mission we’re serving.

Some donors might be giving money because they want to be seen at a gala, or there’s an element of social climbing: I’ll give to your charity and you’ll give to mine. I’ve had donors give me a token gift to see how I thank them, like am I sharing updates about where their gift is going? Am I staying in touch? Sometimes you get people who want their name on a building and it’s not something you can give them. I’ve had to say, “Look, we can’t do that because it’ll put us into a challenging spot with other funders. How can we find other ways to involve you? Can you be involved in the ribbon-cutting?” The people-pleasing can be exhausting. But when you do this work, that’s your challenge: How can I get this person who’s really difficult to invest in my organization?

I cannot tell you how often I’m asked to give fashion advice to development officers. They want to know if they should wear a skirt or pants or a blazer. Many executive directors I work with are women of color, and they’re often walking into a room full of older white businessmen. I always tell people they need to wear what will make them most comfortable. If you are worrying about your jacket or you’re itchy, then they will be able to tell you’re not comfortable. You have to feel good.

There can also be a lot of issues with boundaries, especially between fundraisers, who are predominantly young and female, and donors, who are often older and male. There’s a real power imbalance there. If you’re doing your job right as a fundraiser, it feels to donors like a two-way relationship, but it should really be one-way. Things get messy all the time because you’re dealing with money and power. When I was young, male donors would say things like, “Oh, can we go get a drink after the event?” My first boss made it very clear that I should not get into situations like that. But it’s uncomfortable. You’re trying to woo these people, and they might take it the wrong way.
“I remember thinking, Dude, $10,000 is nothing for you. What is your problem?”— Mallory Erickson, author of What the Fundraising and host of the What the Fundraising podcast

I started my career in the nonprofit sector, and as I got promoted, I found myself in roles that came with fundraising responsibilities. I was very uncomfortable fundraising at first. It was frustrating to be in conversations with people who didn’t recognize these disparities in the world that were so clear to me. I remember thinking, Dude, $10,000 is nothing for you. What is your problem? I was walking away from conversations feeling resentful and pissed off. Unsurprisingly, I was not fundraising very effectively at that time.

I managed to get over that when I realized philanthropy is not necessarily about generosity. It’s often about control. For a lot of people with financial means and power, giving is about exerting their power in a different way — and getting a tax benefit from it. It’s about naming rights and ego and who you get to sit with at lunch. Realizing that made me less disillusioned. The irony is it also helped me meet amazingly generous, wonderful, incredible people who had tremendous wealth and who really wanted to make change in the world. In that sense, fundraising began to feel more like a partnership. A donor’s asset is money and my asset is understanding a problem incredibly well and being in a position to solve it.

A lot of nonprofits are so desperate these days that they’ll bend over backwards to keep donors happy, but it’s not always a good use of resources to do that. Many people don’t see the tremendous amount of pressure fundraisers are under. They have all these deadlines and key performance indicators to hit. A lot of nonprofits have lost federal grants and are truly scrambling right now.

Fundraising can lead to burnout — there’s isolation and rejection and uncertainty and pressure but also power dynamics. Feeling like you’re in a place where you have less power is extremely dysregulating. The financial disparity is acute, but it’s even more pronounced for fundraisers because we see the full spectrum of wealth and need. It’s jarring to be making $40,000 a year at a nonprofit that has to do budget cuts and then going to a big gala full of very wealthy people. When I started out in this field, I didn’t have the consciousness or language to understand that dynamic or why it made me feel so awful. I remember changing my outfit in a car before going into an event with donors and it was stressful. It was just like, Make sure they like you!
Email your money conundrums to mytwocents@nymag.com (and read our submission terms here.)

Back in the halcyon Obama-era days of The Good Wife, when the lawyers at Lockhart & Gardner took on a case that intersected with the burgeoning tech industry, the show’s creators Robert and Michelle King often refracted a real story about Google, Facebook, or Amazon through the prism of a fictional conglomerate known as ChumHum. Created by a Zuckerberg-ish guy named Neil Gross (John Benjamin Hickey), ChumHum got itself entangled in fights over the secrecy of its search-engine algorithm, price-fixing its employees’ salaries, Gross’s marital woes, the theft of a prototype tablet very much like an iPad, and, later on, the algorithmic discrimination propagated by “ChummyMaps.” By the time of the Trump administration, as tech companies got in bed with oppressive regimes, the Kings devoted an episode of follow-up series The Good Fight to ChumHum’s modifying its search results to appease Chinese censors, including a meta bit in which they posted a disclaimer that CBS itself had censored an animated short they’d planned to include.

All of this is to say that if you’ve ever appreciated a Good Wife or Fight episode about ChumHum, or are even just now laughing about the concept of a tech company named ChumHum, you will love the Kings’ new drama, Cupertino, a legal procedural that rehomes the zany, angsty fun of The Good Wife and Fight and more than a little of the existential dread of Evil to America’s current heart of darkness in Northern California. The story kicks off with a team-up between two castoffs of big tech: a pedigreed lawyer named Michael Price, played by Mike Colter (a regular of the Kings’ dramas), who has been kicked out of a start-up he co-founded, and a fresh-out-of-school but sharp Christian lawyer named Olivia Siffre (Rachel Keller), cut from the same company after rebuffing sexual advances from the other co-founder. To get their revenge, the two team up to found their own firm and stick it to the Goliaths of tech.

Michael and Olivia are factory-standard templates of the Kings’ universe: earnest repositories for exposition who aren’t especially engaging themselves but get interesting when paired with more idiosyncratic characters. Their upstart firm, which operates out of Potemkin offices that have more fake walls than actual employees, takes on a receptionist who becomes their investigator, a sardonic, harder-partying variant of The Good Wife’s Marissa Gold played by Ella Stiller (of The Comeback and being Ben’s daughter). Soon, there’s an infusion of cash and chaos from a big benefactor: Busy Philipps, playing a character named Natalia Boutella, who’s the ex of a tech kingpin (a peevish Fisher Stevens) and answers the question, “What if MacKenzie Scott were blonde and had a law degree and an ax to grind with it?”

The weirdness of Cupertino follows a curve of exponential growth. The first few episodes present material that could’ve been on The Good Wife, including a few cases of the week that are shopworn but fun enough; in one, Michael and Olivia represent a put-upon coder played by Nik Dodani, who quickly becomes their resident expert on explaining technobabble. Soon, however, the Kings’ fondness for probing the strangest possible intersections of legal practice pushes Cupertino in odd and hilarious directions. One episode takes place with the characters all calling into a Zoom while stuck in traffic to debate an AI algorithm’s decision to assign an organ to one donor over the other. (In a classic network-drama twist, midway through the episode, evidence emerges that forces the legal teams to switch arguments while still stuck in traffic.)

Cupertino also continues the Kings’ tradition of hiring great New York theater actors to play guest roles, often as rival lawyers and judges. When Michael and Olivia take on a music service duplicating artists’ work to get more streams, the presiding voice from the bench is nine-time Tony winner Danny Burstein, who turns out to be a Parrothead bummed that slop has infiltrated his playlist of Jimmy Buffett favorites. And, in what turns out to be an essential acid ingredient in the Cupertino recipe, Price and Siffre often find themselves going up against a lawyer for a boutique firm representing the mutual interests of the big guys. Played by a fantastically slinky and devious Renée Elise Goldsberry, Nichole E. Ferebee channels elements of Girls5eva’s Wickie Roy and the devil’s associate Lola on Damn Yankees and has sparkling chemistry with Price, often tempting him to return to corporate life. If these companies have become so all-powerful, why not give up the fight and join them?

Given the accelerating nature of the industry Cupertino covers — both in terms of how quickly these companies can innovate and how quickly they can bludgeon regulation around their work into the shape they want — a broadcast show about Silicon Valley occasionally feels a step off from reality. A recurring figure in the first set of episodes is a seemingly self-aware chatbot named Bo (played by an unsettlingly chipper Rob McClure), who becomes a client of the central firm, even when nobody is sure this is actually legal. (He pays them in bitcoin.) Bo comes off as a fantastical vision of AI consciousness, a creation that is either way too ahead of what is possible or, if you’ve just read an article about Anthropic and OpenAI potentially leading us to doomsday, maybe too cuddly and humane. But if there’s inevitable imprecision in the specifics of Cupertino’s plotlines, the sprawling, maximal nature of broadcast television allows it to take a vast survey of the texture and culture of the world it covers that’s mostly accurate (at least based on the ten episodes of season one’s whopping 20-episode order that were shared with critics).

Silicon Valley has developed its own strange niches and cultures, which gives the Kings and their writers a lot of material to work with: There are legal experts calling in from nude parties at Burning Man, AI cults that all but resemble fringe corners of effective altruism, weirdo antisocial billionaires obsessed with building bunkers. There, broadcast television, which has become its own kind of underdog in the streaming age, gets its revenge against the titan that consumed it. Look at these weirdos who rule the world now, Cupertino argues. Don’t they make for great television? They may have subsumed much of our lives into their ever-growing monopolies, but that can’t stop us from laughing at them every week.

When Donald Trump named Kimberly Guilfoyle the U.S. ambassador to Greece in late 2024, the prevailing wisdom was that it had less to do with her diplomatic bona fides than it did her being the ex-fiancée of Donald Trump Jr., who had maybe cheated on her with his now wife. It also probably wasn’t related to, say, a deep knowledge of the Mediterranean, or a reputation for unshakeable ethics, as a new report involving a donor, Kid Rock, a request for a $100,000 wire, and repeated pleas not to leave a paper trail would suggest.
A Wall Street Journal investigation about Guilfoyle’s relationship with Trump donor, failed Kentucky congressional candidate, and former lawyer Eric Deters reveals:
Guilfoyle was under financial stress before taking the Greece posting

In between Trump’s first and second terms, Guilfoyle launched an “upscale vodka and champagne brand” that she tried to drum up money for at a Mar-a-Lago dinner. (She was unsuccessful and dissolved the company.) In the run-up to her confirmation hearing, she reportedly told friends she was broke and, in February 2025 financial disclosures, declared liabilities for a boat loan between $100,000 and $250,000 and a mortgage worth between $1 million and $5 million.

In a text sent last March to Deters — who had previously paid Guilfoyle and then-fiancé Trump Jr. hundreds of thousands of dollars to attend an event protesting COVID medical mandates — Guilfoyle reportedly told him, “I have a lot shit to get done before [moving to Greece] and I need to make money.”
Deters wanted help with “some personal tax and legal issues,” and Guilfoyle was happy to oblige
According to the Journal, Deters promised as much as $1 million to Guilfoyle if she could get him face time with influential members of the Trump administration.

At the Justice Department, he wanted to convince the government to extradite an Ohio doctor who had reportedly “fled to Pakistan after being charged with defrauding insurers by performing unnecessary spinal surgeries, including on children.” He also wanted the DoJ to investigate the doctor’s malpractice insurer MedPro Group, which accused him of “a calculated scheme to extract payments” from the company, “at first through abusive litigation, and by ultimately outright extortion through threats of violence and murder and by blackmail against the company’s CEO.” (Deters denied the accusations to the Journal.)

With Billy Long, the incoming commissioner of the IRS, he wanted to chat about a probe of a 2020 deduction he took connected to the sale of his part of a family business, a probe he believed was politically motivated.

Deters also reportedly offered Guilfoyle $1 million if she could land him an interview on Tucker Carlson’s podcast. And he wanted an introduction to Kid Rock to discuss a song he’d written called “Kentucky Outlaw,” which included the lyrics “He’s a Kentucky outlaw / He fights the man and refuses to crawl.”
Guilfoyle reached out to the IRS commissioner and Tucker Carlson on Deters’s behalf

Text messages seen by the Journal showed “Guilfoyle reached out to people in Carlson’s orbit about setting up an interview with him for Deters.” (Carlson told the publication he’d never heard of Deters and that Guilfoyle plays no role in his guest selection.) Separately, she sent a letter to Long in which she wrote, “Don Jr. and I are very close with Eric Deters and his wife and I know he sent you a letter. I am hoping I know how busy you are that you could give some time and attention to it.” She later texted Deters that Long had responded, writing, “Boom.” According to the Journal, she also “promised to lobby top Trump officials from FBI director Kash Patel to former Attorney General Pam Bondi.” It’s not clear if she made contact with Kid Rock.
Guilfoyle also told Deters to ixnay on the ittenwray videnceyay

In multiple exchanges, Guilfoyle urged Deters to stop referencing their deal in writing. In January 2025, she excoriated him for apparently telling a podcast producer about their deal, saying: “It’s unbelievable when we have a private arrangement with you that you would now CC a producer talking about money. Do not say we have any arrangement … What a nightmare you’ll literally cost me my ambassadorship stop writing.”

In June 2025, Deters sent Guilfoyle a message in which he said, “I have paid you $300,000 over the years. As of this memo, I have not received one favor. I am not naive or a sucker. I need results.” She reportedly responded by telling him to “stop papering all these things. It’s really dangerous,” adding: “Just call me on signal.” In a separate message, she wrote: “Also very privately, if you write an email or a text about, l’m gonna kill you cause I love you but you’re so out of control.”
“I need you to get this done for me today”

In July 2025, Guilfoyle reportedly pressed Deters to send her $100,000 ASAP, to pay down her credit-card balance. “Honey please I need you to get this done for me today,” she allegedly texted him, and then included a prayer-hands emoji and instructions on how to directly wire the money to her American Express account. “You could just send it here,” she said via Signal.

Deters wrote back: “Your needing $100,000 urgent unfortunately is not going to work. I can’t do this without getting a divorce.” Guilfoyle responded, “I’ve been calling you for over a week straight. You could be here meeting with Billy Long.” (Long is now the ambassador to Iceland; the State Department did not respond to the Journal’s request for comment on his behalf.)

Just as an aside, a little backstory on Deters. In 2020 he was banned from an Ohio courthouse because he’d threatened to burn it down. He was twice suspended by the Kentucky Bar Association, which claimed, per the Journal, that he’d engaged in “aggressive litigation strategies, false statements in court proceedings and filing frivolous claims.” During the period in which the Kentucky Supreme Court was weighing whether or not to reinstate his license, Deters called the association’s members “jokes of human excrement.”
Speaking to the Journal, Deters said he’d retired as a lawyer, calling himself a “legal outlaw.”
Marco Rubio is just going to pretend none of this is happening

Speaking to reporters in Greece on Thursday, the secretary of State said, “You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it’s the gospel. It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me. That’s not the way we do things.” At a joint news conference with the Greek foreign minister, he declared, “our embassy here is doing a great job. Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here.”

A facial mass detected before birth prompted the early delivery of identical twin sisters. A fetal MRI at 33 weeks showed the mass on one baby's face. When the sisters were born a week later, tumors were found in both.
Two children had the same cancer, raising a question that their shared beginnings alone could not answer.
Had the disease started separately in each sister, or had cancer cells crossed from one to the other before birth?

Researchers turned to a record hidden within their cells. DNA changes, accumulated as their bodies developed, allowed the team to reconstruct events that had happened months before anyone saw a tumor.

The study in Nature Communications shows that the cancer began in one sister and passed to the other in the womb, most likely through a single transfer late in the second trimester. The same investigation uncovered clues to how the sisters themselves had formed.

The two girls, Amelia and Amaya, died soon after birth. Their family consented to post-mortem examinations for research. The authors dedicate the study to the sisters, whose mother wanted them acknowledged by name.
The team included researchers from the Wellcome Sanger Institute, Great Ormond Street Hospital and the University of Cambridge.

The baby with the facial mass is called twin A in the paper. At birth, she had tumor deposits in several organs. Her sister, twin B, initially had lesions in her skin; disease involving the membranes around the brain and spinal cord was detected later.

The tumors were reported as undifferentiated sarcomas. Soft tissue sarcomas arise in tissues such as muscle, fat and the body's supporting structures. All the twins' tumor samples carried the same fusion of two genes, MN1 and ZNF341.
Matching tumors were only the beginning: the team needed to identify whose cells had started the cancer.
Here, an apparent contradiction proved useful: identical twins are not necessarily genetically identical.

They begin with the same fertilized egg, but DNA changes can arise as their cells multiply. A change acquired by one cell can pass to its descendants, marking a particular branch of the developing body's cellular family tree.
Comparing those marks across tissues reveals shared ancestors and distinguishes one twin's cells from her sister's.
The team sequenced 10 tumor samples, 12 normal tissue samples from the twins and 11 placental samples. They also examined 12 placental samples enriched for cells involved in forming the placenta.

The researchers found that cancer began in twin A, then cancer cells passed to twin B before birth and formed tumors there too. The evidence was in the second baby's tumors: their cells carried genetic markers belonging to her sister.
The study points to spread across the placenta they shared. The genetic analysis establishes which sister the cancer came from, but does not directly show the cells crossing or the route they took.

The most likely starting site was twin A's facial mass. The cancer diversified into different cell populations and spread within her body before reaching her sister. The pattern in twin B supported a relatively late, single transfer.

The researchers then used accumulated mutations to estimate when this happened. Assuming mutations built up at a constant rate, they placed the tumor's origin near the end of the first trimester and its transfer late in the second trimester.
Those dates are estimates that depend on the assumed mutation rate, rather than direct observations.

There was another surprise: normal cells had moved in the opposite direction. Genetic markers in a spleen sample from twin A suggested around 75 percent of the sampled cells originated in twin B, consistent with blood-cell mixing between the sisters.

The twins' earliest cell lineages also contributed unevenly to their bodies and placenta. One branch contributed almost exclusively to twin A, another to both sisters and the placenta, and a third to twin B and the placenta. The pattern favored an earlier embryonic split than the classical model for this type of identical twinning predicts.
However, this was one pair of twins, and the analysis could recover only lineages that survived in the tissues sampled.

Earlier research on twins with leukemia has also explored cancer's beginnings before birth. This case adds a detailed reconstruction of a soft tissue tumor's journey, without establishing how often such transfers occur.

Nor does the study show that a cancer in one twin must reach the other. The researchers interpret the transfer as a rare event, rather than an unavoidable consequence of the sisters sharing their prenatal environment.
The approach offers a way to investigate the developmental origins of childhood tumors alongside normal growth.
The research has been published in Nature Communications.
The Air Force’s B-52 bomber may soon be able to carry up to 20 stealthy long-range anti-ship missiles to strike moving targets at sea, a key capability in a potential fight with China.
An Oct. 7 notice from Naval Air Systems Command states that the command plans to award a contract to Lockheed Martin to integrate its Long-Range Anti-Ship Missile on the B-52.

The anticipated award “is for efforts associated with LRASM integration on the B-52 aircraft platform, to include missile software updates, associated testing, test asset repair, and failure review boards,” the notice states.
The B-52 can already carry up to 20 Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missiles, on which the LRASM is based. The two missiles share similar dimensions.

Naval News first reported on the possibility of integrating the LRASM onto the B-52 in 2019, though the idea languished for several years. But the ability to put LRASMs on the B-52 would have massive implications in a large-scale conflict, retired Air Force Col. Mark Gunzinger, a former B-52 pilot, told Air & Space Forces Magazine.

“A handful of B-52s will be able to deliver more weapons on maritime targets and do so over much longer ranges than the Navy’s carrier-based aircraft per day,” said Gunzinger, now as the director of future concepts and capability assessments for the Mitchell Institute of Aerospace Studies.

Spokespeople for NAVAIR and Air Force Life Cycle Management Center did not immediately responded to a request for comment. Lockheed spokesperson Scott Swofford declined to provide any further details about the effort, deferring to the Pentagon, but did tout LRASM’s capabilities.

“As a precise, stealthy and survivable cruise missile, LRASM provides multiservice, multiplatform, and multimission capabilities for offensive anti-surface warfare,” Swofford said. “By leveraging Lockheed Martin’s expertise in successful cruise missile productions, LRASM brings low-risk and long-term, flexible capabilities to the warfighters’ anti-surface warfare environment that no other inventory weapon provides.”

The Oct. 7 notice continues a push to integrate LRASM onto the bomber fleet—the Air Force revealed in June that a B-2A Spirit employed a LRASM to strike a decommissioned amphibious transport vessel during a Pacific exercise, the first time the U.S. military has acknowledged the B-2’s use of that missile.
Such a pairing is important, Gunzinger said.

“The Air Force’s bomber force will be our military’s predominant maritime strike force, considering the number of anti-ship cruise missiles they can carry per sortie and deliver over intercontinental ranges, if necessary,” Gunzinger said. “And LRASMs will give our bomber force the ability to strike moving targets at sea with unprecedented accuracy.”
The move will expand commanders’ options to strike maritime targets while launching from airbases in lower threat density areas, he said, without putting aircraft carriers at risk.
- 2009: DARPA and the U.S. Navy initiate the program to develop advanced anti-ship strike capabilities.
- 2012: DARPA cancels the supersonic LRASM-B variant to focus exclusively on the subsonic, stealthy LRASM-A based on the JASSM-ER.
- 2013: Lockheed Martin completes the first successful air-launch flight test of the missile from a USAF B-1B bomber.
- 2015: The Pentagon officially designates the stealthy anti-ship missile as the AGM-158C.
- 2017: Lockheed Martin receives the first low-rate initial production contract
- 2018: The U.S. Air Force achieves Early Operational Capability with the AGM-158C on the B-1B Lancer.
- 2019: The U.S. Navy achieves Early Operational Capability integrating the missile onto F/A-18E/F Super Hornets.
- 2024: The U.S. Navy completes four-missile salvo testing and begins flight testing the round on the F-35C
- 2025: Initial flight testing expands to the F-35B short-takeoff/vertical-landing variant.
- 2026: Lockheed Martin expands factory capacity and contract modifications to boost annual production.
Sources: Lockheed Martin, Air & Space Forces Magazine, USNI
Lockheed produces both the the AGM-158 JASSM and the AGM-158C LRASM. There is also the AGM-158-JASSM Extended Range variant, which can hit targets out to 500 miles.
Currently, the B-1B Lancer, B-2A Spirit, B-52H Stratofortress, F-15 variants, F-16 variants, and C-130 Hercules can carry the JASSM.
The Air Force is also integrating the JASSM onto the F-35A Lightning II and the B-21 Raider.
The LRASM’s range hovers close to the baseline JASSM variant, just beyond 200 miles.
Air & Space Forces Magazine recently reported on JASSM and LRASM production progress based on Pentagon acquisition reports released in July.

The reports noted that, as of April, the Navy and Air Force were expanding their production plans for the shared munition. Lockheed had delivered a total of 5,348 JASSMs to both services. The company’s current production capacity is 600 JASSMs a year, with short-term plans to boost that to 860 missiles annually.
That’s key, as a recent Center for a New American Security report estimates that the Air Force has ripped through a quarter of its JASSM inventory during Operation Epic Fury.

Lockheed announced a new AGM-158 JASSM-FLEX variant in September at the AFA Air, Space & Cyber conference. The new variant lets users swap out the nose and launch options for various payloads and other configuration needs, which might include an LRASM option.

“The AGM-158 FLEX airframe concept was driven by a strategic need to keep pace with rapidly evolving threats, insert emerging technologies quickly, manage obsolescence, and provide, at scale, a cost-effective missile family that can be repurposed for a wide range of missions while delivering timely, relevant capability to the warfighter,” a Lockheed Martin spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine via email.

The Air Force spent $200 million in fiscal 2025 for a second-source engine for the LRASM and JASSM-ER. Lockheed plans to spend between $8 and $9 million through 2030 to boost production on existing lines.

ESA astronaut Sophie Adenot returned to Earth with Crew-12 after her nearly eight-month εpsilon mission to the International Space Station, splashing down off the coast of California, USA, at 15:34 GMT/17:34 CEST on 8 October 2026.

Sophie, together with NASA astronauts Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway and Roscosmos cosmonaut Andrei Fedyaev, undocked on 7 October at 12:05 GMT/14:05 CEST, beginning a 27 hours and 29 minutes return journey back to Earth.
The splashdown took place near Los Angeles, off the coast of California, where joint SpaceX/NASA/ESA/ROSCOSMOS recovery crews were waiting for the Dragon Freedom spacecraft.

After re-entering the Earth’s atmosphere and slowing down from around 28 000 km/h to about 500 km/h, the drogue chutes deployed at an altitude of about 5500 m, followed by the four main chutes approximately one minute later.

After the splashdown, fast boat teams immediately headed toward the Dragon capsule, reaching it within minutes to perform safety checks. The team aboard the SpaceX recovery vessel Shannon lifted Dragon aboard before opening the side hatch and helping each crew member out of the spacecraft.
Sophie was the third to exit the spacecraft, smiling and celebrating after her first, record-breaking spaceflight.

Following initial medical checks aboard the recovery vessel, Sophie and her crewmates will travel to shore by helicopter before boarding a NASA plane at the nearest airport for the flight to Ellington Field in Houston and their initial post-flight activities.
From there, Sophie will board a plane to ESA’s European Astronaut Centre (EAC) in Cologne, Germany.

Sophie spent a total of 237 days, 5 hours and 18 minutes in space after being launched on 13 February 2026 from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida, USA. The εpsilon mission set a new European record for the longest single spaceflight, exceeding by more than 35 days the previous record held by ESA astronaut Luca Parmitano for his Beyond mission.

Sophie is the second European woman, after ESA astronaut Samantha Cristoforetti, and the first French woman to conduct an Extra Vehicular Activity (EVA), or spacewalk. Sophie completed three spacewalks in 14 days, spending a total of 19 hours and 42 minutes working outside the Station.

Throughout εpsilon, Sophie carried out a wide range of European experiments spanning fields from health research to materials science, biology, fluid physics, radiation physics and fundamental science.

Alongside this broad research programme, Sophie also helped to test technologies for future exploration missions, including the new European exercise device E4D and in-orbit metal 3D printing, and supported commercial research payloads.

A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket took off on a flight to the International Space Station Thursday carrying two NASA astronauts, a cosmonaut and a Canadian whose wife plans a launch of her own later this year, giving birth to the couple’s third child while her husband is away in space.

Strapped into a SpaceX Crew Dragon capsule, Crew 13 commander Jessica Watkins, pilot Luke Delaney, Russian cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov and Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk blasted off from pad 40 at the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station at 11:10 a.m. EDT.
The launch originally was planned for mid September, but the flight was delayed to replace a leaking valve in the Crew Dragon’s propulsion system.

Watkins, who holds a Ph.D. in geology, flew to space aboard a Crew Dragon in 2022. Her crewmates are space rookies, the 296th, 297th and 298th astronauts to fly aboard the ISS. Delaney and Kutryk are both former military test pilots while Teteryatnikov served in the Russian submarine force before becoming a cosmonaut.

Kutryk and his wife Heather have two children, ages 5 and 7. They’re expecting their third child around Thanksgiving, about two months into the Crew 13 mission. In so doing, they will become the fourth couple in space history to have a child born while one parent was off the planet.

“Leaving these three (plus one on the way) is the hardest thing I’ve ever done,” Kutryk wrote in a post on the social media platform X. “But that has always been the nature of exploration.” He then quoted Norwegian arctic explorer Fridtjof Nansen, describing his thoughts upon setting off for the North Pole.

“‘Behind me lay all I held dear in life. And what lay before me? Happy child, little do you know what life is — how strangely mingled and how full of change… and now, a farewell to home. It was the darkest hour of the whole journey.'”

Despite President Trump’s recent animosity toward Canada, the Canadian Space Agency continues to play a major role in the U.S. space program. Along with supplying the robot arms that helped build the space station, CSA astronaut Jeremy Hansen flew around the moon on NASA’s Artemis II mission. Kutryk is the 17th Canadian to fly in space.

“When I think about the space station, I hope the legacy is that people see this beacon in the sky going around Earth, one of the most complex things humans have ever, ever created, and they see it for all of its technical marvel and all the science and discoveries we’re making there,” he said.

“But (I hope) they also see it as sort of this beacon for what we can do when we make good decisions, when we work together and we collaborate and we prioritize things. It’s testament to what we’ve done, what we can do, and really to what we hope the generations that follow can do.”

After boosting the Falcon 9 and Crew Dragon capsule out of the dense lower atmosphere, the Falcon 9’s first stage flew itself back to a pinpoint landing at the Space Force station while the rocket’s upper stage continued the climb to space. Minutes later, the second stage engine shut down and the crew capsule separated to fly on its own.

“What an epic ride!” Delaney radioed. “What an epic ride it was! Today, we proudly continue the streak of humans living and working in orbit, building on the legacies of yesterday to pave the way for future of space exploration … Deepest appreciation to my family and friends who stood by me throughout this entire endeavor. Thank you. I love you guys. And to the Marines back on Earth, Semper Fi.”

Like all flights to the International Space Station, piloted and unpiloted alike, the Crew 13 launch was timed for the moment Earth’s rotation carried the pad into the plane of the station’s orbit. That’s a requirement for rendezvous missions because no current rockets have the power to overcome their orbital momentum and change their direction of travel when moving at nearly 5 miles per second.

While a Falcon 9 cannot change orbital planes, the Crew Dragon capsule can change its altitude as required, flying lower — and faster — to catch up with its quarry and higher to slow down the approach.

In this case, it will take Crew 13 capsule just eight hours — a NASA record — to catch up with the ISS, moving in for an automated docking at the forward port of the station’s Harmony module at 7 p.m.

“I personally am looking forward to returning to the ISS as well as flying on Dragon a second time, and really looking forward to experiencing those experiences through the eyes of my crewmates,” Watkins said.

“We expect a very busy mission with lots of station maintenance, both internal and external, with a few EVAs (spacewalks) on the docket as well as visiting vehicle capture and stowage operations, lots of science … and plenty of outreach.”

Standing by to welcome Watkins and company aboard will be the crew they are replacing: Crew 12 commander Jessica Meir, pilot Jack Hathaway, European Space Agency astronaut Sophie Adenot and cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev. They’re wrapping up a 235-day mission that began with launch atop a Falcon 9 rocket on Feb. 13.
Godspeed Crew-13! pic.twitter.com/W3r5aeAPHg
— Jessica Meir (@Astro_Jessica) October 1, 2026

Also on board: Soyuz MS-29/75S cosmonauts Pyotr Dubrov, Anna Kikina and NASA astronaut Anil Menon, launched on a Soyuz 2.1a rocket from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan on July 14. They’re in the midst of an eight-month stay, returning to Earth in early April 2027.

After an expedited “crew handover,” during which Meir and her crewmates will show their replacements the ins and outs of station operations, Crew 12 will board their own Crew Dragon capsule and return to Earth. Undocking is planned for Oct. 5 with splashdown in the Pacific Ocean off the southern California coast on Oct. 6.

“I think the thing that I’m looking forward to most is seeing my three-and-a-half-year-old daughter,” said Meir, a two-flight veteran with seven spacewalks to her credit. “I’m so looking forward to seeing nature again, feeling the breeze on my face, the wind rustling through the leaves, experiencing all those things that we don’t have up here.
“But I will very, very much miss being weightless all the time and the incredible views that we have.”

Said Hathaway: “Going home and being able to take a nice long hot shower will be very relaxing and very nice. And, of course, I’m looking forward to seeing my family. But a hot shower is near the top of my list.”

Crew 12’s departure will free up the Harmony module’s space-facing port for the arrival of a SpaceX Cargo Dragon on Oct. 13 that will be loaded with crew supplies, science gear, spare parts and two roll-out solar array panels. The Crew 13 fliers also expect to welcome a Northrop Grumman cargo ship in December, along with two Russian Progress freighters in November and February.

The roll-out solar arrays going up on the next Dragon Cargo ship are the final sets in a major upgrade to the station’s original solar power system that began with initial installations in June 2021. The final two sets will be installed during spacewalks late this month and early November.
Dragon separates from Falcon 9’s second stage pic.twitter.com/Ay7VmubfF6

But the major goal of the flight, like all NASA missions to the station, is conducting research in the microgravity environment of space. Scores of experiments and technology demonstrations are running at any given moment with fresh studies going up on virtually every flight.
The Crew 13 fliers will face the same challenges.

“During the mission, the crew will help us fight heart disease and Parkinson’s disease by studying human stem cell-derived tissues that will help improve medicine, disease modeling, and pharmaceutical testing,” said Dana Weigel, director of NASA’s low-Earth orbit mission directorate.

“They will also explore crop production that’s important for longer-duration spaceflight missions, and they’ll help us better understand blood flow abnormalities that we see in space, along with testing new diagnostic medical equipment for monitoring crew health. That’s just a couple of the highlights of the research the crew will be doing on board.”
All in all, Hathaway said, the crew is looking forward to an action-packed stay in space.

“For me, between the science, the spacewalks and everything else that the expedition is going to have, it’s looking to be a great time,” Delaney said. “Excited to launch with this crew, join the expedition, and integrate as an extension of NASA and all the ISS team members. So exciting times ahead!”

NASA’s SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization, and Ices Explorer) space telescope is shedding light on brown dwarfs, celestial objects that blur the line between stars and exoplanets. New findings published in The Astrophysical Journal show that these dark and cloudy worlds have chemically rich atmospheres not unlike the giant planets in our own solar system.

First discovered in the 1990s, brown dwarfs form from collapsing clouds of gas, like stars do, but they aren’t hefty enough to sustain hydrogen fusion in their cores. These dimly glowing balls of warm gas also share characteristics with Jupiter and Saturn. In contrast to most planets, however, brown dwarfs drift in darkness, ungoverned by a host star and heated entirely from within.

“They’re kind of goth,” said Zafar Rustamkulov, lead author of the new study and a scientist at IPAC, Caltech’s science and data center in Pasadena, California. “Unlike exoplanets, free-floating brown dwarfs are completely independent celestial objects that will fade into eternity alone. We’re still learning how complex they are.”

Only a few dozen of these “dark wanderers” have been studied in detail with space-based telescopes. Astronomers want to observe more of them in the wild because much of our understanding of their makeup, storminess, and evolution comes from theoretical models.
Enter NASA’s SPHEREx, an infrared space telescope launched in March 2025 and managed by the agency’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California.

The study authors analyzed SPHEREx observations of 37 nearby brown dwarfs spanning the full brown dwarf temperature range, from about 4,000 to minus 10 degrees Fahrenheit (2,200 to minus 20 degrees Celsius). The telescope measures their brightness in 102 different colors, from the deepest red our eyes can see, to the invisible heat of infrared light, creating a spectrum. These spectra revealed to the study authors chemically rich atmospheres harboring water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and methane.

“We’re seeing the signatures of these molecules and how they change from object to object across the entire temperature regime,” said study coauthor J. Davy Kirkpatrick, a scientist at Caltech’s IPAC. “Our paper concentrated on just three dozen, but we have thousands more that we are in the process of analyzing. I really want to see what bounds the universe places on the variety of brown dwarfs.”

“From orbit, SPHEREx sees wavelengths of light that are basically impossible to see with telescopes on the ground because water in Earth’s atmosphere absorbs them,” Rustamkulov said. “We are picking up light from the deep, red clouds of brown dwarfs all over the sky.”

Spotting brown dwarfs is something of a side project for SPHEREx. The space telescope takes about 3,600 unique images per day to stitch into maps of the entire sky. Knowing where hundreds of millions of galaxies are distributed across the cosmos will help scientists reconstruct what happened in the first billionth of a trillionth of a trillionth of a second after the big bang. As it scans the sky, the telescope also is searching for the chemical ingredients of life and finding interstellar ice that could one day seed oceans on distant worlds.

For years, brown dwarfs have been spotted by other observatories, including NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope and retired Spitzer Space Telescope. But thanks to its spectral coverage, SPHEREx is now imaging thousands of them for the first time in a fruitful region of the electromagnetic spectrum that spans deep red and infrared wavelengths of light.

At those wavelengths, molecules carve out distinct absorption patterns in the light shining out to space. The patterns change as brown dwarfs grow older and colder. Some of the brown dwarfs observed by SPHEREx are in a dynamic stage of life when their exotic clouds thin out, giving way to methane-rich atmospheres.

“The state-of-the-art models are capturing the general chemical trend, but when it comes to these cloudy transitions, the models are struggling to match the data,” said Rustamkulov. “No two brown dwarfs are alike. Even at the same temperature, their spectra look quite distinct.”

“The findings are a call to action to explore even more of these dark worlds,” said Kirkpatrick. “This journey has turned many of us into accidental meteorologists. We know how hard it is to predict weather on our own planet, and we realize it’s going to be just as challenging to explain the phenomena we see in these bizarre, cold objects.”

The mission is managed by JPL for NASA’s Astrophysics Division within the Science Mission Directorate in Washington. The telescope and the spacecraft bus were built by BAE Systems. The science analysis of the SPHEREx data is being conducted by a team of scientists at 13 institutions across the United States and in South Korea and Taiwan, led by Jamie Bock, principal investigator, who is based at Caltech with a joint JPL appointment, and by JPL’s Olivier Doré, the project scientist. Data is processed and archived at IPAC at Caltech in Pasadena. Caltech manages JPL for NASA. The SPHEREx dataset is freely available to scientists and the public.
